grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: hay agua; hay dos libros. El agua está cerca; los libros están lejos.
grammar.note_en:
Hay introduces the existence or presence of something: Hay agua en el suelo de la sala means “There is water on the reading-room floor”. It does not mean that the water belongs to the room or that somebody has it. Hay is a form of haber, but this chapter introduces only this impersonal present form. Impersonal means it has no ordinary subject naming a person who performs the action. Do not change hay for a plural noun: Hay dos libros en la misma silla means “There are two books on the same chair”. The same hay serves English “there is” and “there are”.

After hay, the reading commonly introduces an indefinite noun phrase—one not yet identified—or a quantity or substance: Hay un papel mojado, “There is a wet paper”; hay dos libros, “there are two books”; hay agua, “there is water”. An indefinite article such as un/una introduces one member of a class. The absence of an article before agua describes water as a substance. No hay agua aquí means “There is no water here”. ¿Hay agua dentro de la caja, Luis? means “Is there water inside the box, Luis?” Questions and negation leave hay unchanged.

Está and están locate or describe an already identified referent. La caja está seca means “The box is dry”; el agua está cerca del libro means “the water is near the book”; Las manos de Elena están secas means “Elena’s hands are dry”. The verb agrees with its subject: caja and agua take singular está; manos takes plural están. Do not make hay agree with the following books or drops. The contrast is a difference in what the sentence is doing: introducing what exists in a place, or saying where a known thing is. It is not an absolute claim that every indefinite noun must use hay; a Spanish speaker can identify a particular object in other ways. The controlled exercises give a verb cue in parentheses so the required form is clear.

Encima de means “above” or “on top of”; debajo de means “under” or “below”. Encima del libro blanco hay un cuaderno viejo means “On top of the white book there is an old notebook”. Debajo del estante está el suelo mojado means “Below the shelf is the wet floor”. De contracts with el to del, already met in earlier chapters. These are relational expressions: say what something is above or below when context does not supply it. Cerca de is “near”; lejos de is “far from”. La silla está lejos del agua means “The chair is far from the water”. The distance is relative to the object named, not a fixed number of steps. En la pared hay una ventana means “There is a window in the wall”; a gota is a drop, lluvia rain, techo the roof or ceiling, and estante a shelf. The story locates the wet area of the ceiling above the shelf; the closed window is a different feature.

Proteger means “protect”. Luis protege los libros means “Luis protects the books”: he moves the box out of the wet area. Elena protects the notebook and the books by lifting them; Ana protects the already wet inventory paper from further water. Protection does not necessarily mean that an object was never wet, and it is not a synonym of lifting or carrying. This chapter uses protege for a named singular person, a regular third-person form. It does not introduce the first-person spelling. The earlier regular verb recibir now appears as ¿Recibes el cuaderno? (“Are you receiving the notebook?”) and Recibo el cuaderno (“I receive the notebook”); their -es and -o endings follow chapter 4’s pattern.

A cuaderno is a notebook used for writing, unlike the printed reading books. Cuenta here means an account of expenditure, not a tale. En el cuaderno hay una cuenta vieja means “In the notebook there is an old account”. The delivered page shows an older dated repair record and its sums beside the roof and wall labels. That visual record supplies the earlier-work clue without introducing a Spanish past-tense verb. The present reading contrasts an old record with the currently wet ceiling; it has not established who did the work or how to repair the leak. The room’s key remains distinct from the box and cupboard keys. The two new inventory labels from chapter 4 remain distinct from the old account page.

The reference tables translate as follows: hay agua / hay dos libros, “there is water / there are two books”; el agua está cerca / los libros están lejos, “the water is near / the books are far away”; encima del libro / debajo del estante, “on top of the book / under the shelf”; cerca del agua / lejos del agua, “near the water / far from the water”.
